title: NVIDIA RISC-V for NVIDIA GPUs at Hot Chips 2026
gist: At Hot Chips 2026 NVIDIA published the concrete requirements a RISC-V host CPU must meet to run CUDA and to attach via NVLink Fusion — RVA23 profiles, ACPI 6.6, PCIe I/O coherency and peer-to-peer, roughly 88 PCIe lanes, C2C with CHI coherence, plus DOCA and NCCL support — and stated it has plans for RISC-V in its platforms. SiFive is named as the RISC-V NVLink Fusion CPU partner, with broader RISC-V server deployment still perhaps two generations away.

themes.theme: RISC-V as a third server CPU ISA

insights.claim: NVIDIA stated at Hot Chips 2026 that it has plans for RISC-V in its platforms, moving the ISA from lower-level controller duty toward host CPU roles.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: An NVIDIA endorsement is the single strongest demand signal RISC-V server IP can get; it raises the option value of RISC-V core vendors and pressures Arm's datacenter licensing leverage.
insights.quote: “NVIDIA has plans for RISC-V in its platforms” there you go.
insights.locator: NVIDIA closes by making the case

insights.claim: RISC-V is characterized as moving toward a genuine third option in the server CPU market alongside x86 and Arm, on the strength of published integration requirements rather than aspiration.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A credible third ISA compresses pricing power for both x86 incumbents and Arm in server sockets over the next several years.
insights.quote: NVIDIA’s roadmap makes clear that RISC-V is moving toward a genuine third option in the server CPU market alongside x86 and Arm.

insights.claim: Broader RISC-V server processor deployment is estimated to be roughly two hardware generations away despite industry conviction that it is coming.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Sets the timing frame: this is a multi-year option, not a near-term share shift, so fade any 2026-27 RISC-V server volume narrative.
insights.quote: We still are maybe two generations from broader RISC-V processor deployment, but folks in the industry say it is coming.

insights.claim: NVIDIA already uses RISC-V in its current platforms for some lower-level controllers, so the new development is specifically its extension to host CPUs.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Distinguishes embedded microcontroller RISC-V volume, which already exists, from the far larger and still-unwon server host socket.
insights.quote: NVIDIA uses RISC-V in its current platforms for some of the lower-level controllers, but this is a presentation about host CPUs
insights.locator: NVIDIA Advantages of RISC-V for server customers

insights.claim: NVIDIA's argument for RISC-V rests on it being an open standard with multiple vendors that combines standardization with customization, broadening server CPU choice.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor supply is the strategic point for NVIDIA — it wants optionality in host CPUs it does not control, which matters for anyone modeling Arm's dependence on NVIDIA volumes.
insights.locator: NVIDIA closes by making the case for RISC-V

themes.theme: The CUDA compatibility bar for RISC-V

insights.claim: NVIDIA today supports Intel and AMD x86 CPUs plus Arm CPUs as CUDA hosts, so any RISC-V entrant must reach parity with an already complex and heterogeneous host software stack of CUDA libraries, drivers, tools and third-party software.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Software porting, not silicon, is the gating cost for a RISC-V CUDA host — the real barrier to entry investors should track.
insights.quote: NVIDIA already supports Intel/AMD x86 CPUs along with Arm CPUs on the CPU side.
insights.locator: This host CPU software stack is complex and heterogeneous

insights.claim: NVIDIA points to the RVA23 profile and the RISC-V Boot and Runtime Services specification for the application layer, plus RISC-V server SoC and platform specifications at the system level, as the concrete compliance targets for CUDA-capable RISC-V CPUs.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A published spec checklist turns a vague ISA story into a scoreable roadmap; vendors shipping RVA23-compliant server parts are the ones with a path into NVIDIA platforms.
insights.locator: For RISC-V CPUs to run CUDA

insights.claim: The RVA23 profile guarantees key extensions are present so software runs across varied RISC-V processors, directly answering the criticism that RISC-V is a fragmented wild west without a common baseline.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Fragmentation has been the core bear case on RISC-V in servers; profile-based releases materially weaken it.
insights.quote: NVIDIA says the RVA23 profile guarantees key extensions are present, so software runs across a variety of RISC-V processors without a lowest common denominator problem.
insights.locator: Software binary compatibility is a central goal

insights.claim: RISC-V's server platform plumbing is very new: the UEFI Forum added RISC-V support in ACPI 6.6 ratified in May 2025, with the RISC-V Boot and Runtime Services specification following in August 2025.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Only about a year of ecosystem maturation exists behind these specs, which underwrites the two-generation lag estimate for real deployment.
insights.quote: This UEFI Forum added RISC-V support in ACPI 6.6, ratified in May 2025, and the RISC-V Boot and Runtime Services specification followed in August 2025.
insights.locator: ACPI is one example of a RISC-V platform requirement

insights.claim: Hardware PCIe I/O coherency is a CUDA-specific host requirement that NVIDIA sees in most and possibly all modern server CPUs, because it avoids frequent cache flush and invalidate operations and improves latency.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A concrete, non-obvious silicon feature gate — RISC-V designs lacking hardware I/O coherence are disqualified from CUDA hosting regardless of core performance.
insights.quote: Hardware-based PCIe I/O coherence avoids frequent cache flush and invalidate operations.
insights.locator: PCIe coherency is a CUDA-specific requirement

insights.claim: PCIe peer-to-peer communication is the second CUDA-specific requirement, letting a GPU write directly into another GPU's device memory and signal the host by flags, avoiding an extra copy through host memory.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Explains why multi-GPU server topologies have long been unusual, and why platform-level PCIe capabilities gate accelerator scaling.
insights.quote: This was one of the big reasons we saw funky designs in GPU servers even a decade ago.
insights.locator: PCIe peer-to-peer communication is the other CUDA-specific requirement

themes.theme: NVLink Fusion raises the bar further

insights.claim: NVLink Fusion CPUs inherit every CUDA requirement and add more, including a high-speed C2C interconnect with around 88 PCIe lanes plus software support such as DOCA for networking and NCCL for multi-GPU communication.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: An ~88-lane, DOCA/NCCL-capable requirement set narrows the field of credible custom CPU partners to a handful of well-funded programs.
insights.quote: NVIDIA points to a high-speed C2C interconnect with around 88 PCIe lanes and software such as DOCA for networking and NCCL for multi-GPU communication.
insights.locator: NVLink Fusion CPUs inherit all CUDA requirements

insights.claim: SiFive is named as the RISC-V-based NVLink Fusion CPU partner, making it the identified vehicle for RISC-V entering NVIDIA rack platforms.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Concentrates the RISC-V-in-AI-datacenter thesis on one named IP vendor and its licensees rather than the ISA broadly.
insights.quote: SiFive is being noted as the NVLink Fusion CPU partner that is RISC-V based.
insights.locator: NVLink Fusion requirements for custom CPUs

insights.claim: Inside a custom CPU the NVLink C2C PHY provides a CPU-to-GPU high-bandwidth interface with CHI coherence, letting CPU and GPU access all memory under a unified memory architecture.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Coherent unified memory is the technical reason custom CPUs must adopt NVIDIA's interconnect rather than a generic PCIe attach — a durable lock-in mechanism.
insights.quote: This NVLink C2C PHY provides a CPU-to-GPU high-bandwidth interface with CHI coherence.
insights.locator: Inside a custom CPU, NVIDIA shows the C2C interface integration

insights.claim: NVLink Fusion is positioned as the mechanism by which custom silicon connects into the NVIDIA AI platform, with custom CPUs attaching to XPUs over NVLink C2C while the rack retains a single L1 domain.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: NVIDIA monetizes the rack and fabric even when the compute die is someone else's — the structural hedge against custom accelerator adoption.
insights.locator: NVLink Fusion is how custom silicon connects

insights.claim: Vera Rubin is described as a full-stack AI factory platform co-designed across seven chips and five racks, spanning the Vera CPU, Rubin GPU, networking, storage, and a scale-out fabric.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Seven chips and five racks per platform means NVIDIA's per-deployment content is expanding well beyond the GPU, supporting dollar-content growth even at flat GPU counts.
insights.quote: Vera Rubin is a full-stack AI factory platform built through co-design across seven chips and five racks.
insights.locator: Vera Rubin Is a Full-Stack AI Factory Platform

insights.claim: The NVL72 rack packs a 72-GPU L1 domain into a fully copper domain, with each compute tray holding GPUs on NVLink Fusion chiplets alongside two Vera CPUs linked by C2C.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A fully copper 72-GPU domain caps optical content inside the rack while making rack-scale copper cabling and connector suppliers a direct beneficiary.
insights.quote: NVIDIA’s NVL72 rack packs a 72-GPU L1 domain into a fully copper domain.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's own CPU line has moved from Grace to Vera on the Arm ISA, but the platform is presented as much broader than any single in-house CPU.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is deliberately not making its rack dependent on its own Arm CPUs, which is the opening third-party CPU vendors are being invited into.
insights.locator: NVIDIA has its Grace, and now Vera

insights.claim: CUDA dates back to 2006 and splits applications so compute-intensive functions parallelize on the GPU while the remainder runs sequentially on the CPU, a division that keeps a capable host CPU mandatory in every AI system.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The host CPU is not optional in AI servers, so every accelerator deployment carries an attached server CPU socket worth contesting.
insights.quote: Compute-intensive functions are parallelized on the GPU while the rest of the application runs sequentially on the CPU.
insights.locator: CUDA applications split work between CPU and GPU
